verses.translation_literal: To the choirmaster, for Jeduthun. A psalm, of David.
verses.translation_dramatic: For the choirmaster, for Jeduthun's company: a psalm, David's own.
verses.directors_commentary: This heading is part of the Hebrew text and carries a verse number of its own; the KJV prints it unnumbered, which is why every later verse in this psalm sits one number higher in Hebrew than in the English. 'Choirmaster' (lamnatseach) is a performance direction, from a root meaning to oversee or lead. 'Jeduthun' is the name of a Levitical musician of David's time (1 Chr 16:41-42, 25:1-3), and the Hebrew reads 'for Jeduthun', not 'even to Jeduthun' as the KJV supplies, an 'even' that exists only in English. Whether it names the singer's guild, a tune, or an instrument was already debated: Rashi takes a man among the singers, Metzudat Zion an instrument. For the actors: this is a song handed to a professional guild, not a private diary. The private cry that follows was meant to be sung in public.

philological_notes.note: 'For the one who leads, the overseer'; a musical direction found in dozens of psalm headings. The meaning 'choirmaster' is the traditional and common scholarly rendering.

Read (Qere) 'for Jeduthun'; the written form is 'Jeduthun' spelled with a yod. A Levitical singer in David's time (1 Chr 16:41-42); Rashi also records an instrument of that name, and Ibn Ezra a known melody.

verses.translation_literal: I said: I will guard my ways from sinning with my tongue; I will keep for my mouth a muzzle, while yet [the] wicked [is] before me.
verses.translation_dramatic: I told myself: Watch your steps. Guard them, so that my tongue never turns sinner. I will put a muzzle on my own mouth, and keep it there for as long as the wicked stand in front of me.
verses.directors_commentary: The voice begins with an inner resolution, not a prayer: 'I said', meaning 'I said in my heart' (Radak). 'Ways' is the whole manner of living, and the man's plan is to protect it by controlling a single organ. The key word is machsom, a muzzle, the very word used for the ox that treads grain (Deut 25:4, as Rashi and Metzudat Zion note). The KJV softens it to 'bridle', which belongs to a horse and suggests steering; the Hebrew is a device that shuts a mouth so it cannot bite or eat. The speaker treats his own mouth as an animal that might do damage. The reason is 'while the wicked is before me': a hostile onlooker, one who, in Radak's reading, has come to visit and look at the sufferer, and who would be glad of any complaint. The KJV 'wicked' is correct; BBE 'sinner' is weaker. In an honor culture a sick man who cries out against God hands his enemies a confession. Play the first line quietly, between clenched teeth.

philological_notes.note: A muzzle, the device put over the mouth of an animal; the verb is used of not muzzling the threshing ox (Deut 25:4). Stronger than the KJV's 'bridle'.
'My ways': conduct and manner of life, not roads (Radak compares Ps 119:26).

verses.translation_literal: I was made mute [in] silence, I kept still from good, and my pain was stirred up.
verses.translation_dramatic: So I went dumb. Silence closed over me like a lid. I held back even the good word, the kind word, the word that would have cost nothing. And all the while the pain beneath it churned and clouded, as a well is clouded when something moves at the bottom.
verses.directors_commentary:
The speaker piles up three words for quiet in one breath: a passive 'I was made mute', the noun 'silence', and a causative 'I made myself still'. Actors should not play this as calm. It is clamped-down speech, a man holding his jaw shut. The line 'from good' most naturally means 'away from good [speech]': he will not say even something harmless, for fear a complaint slips out beside it (Ibn Ezra, Radak, Metzudat David).

The KJV keeps all three silence words ('dumb', 'with silence', 'held my peace'), so little is lost in the count. What blurs is the verb. 'Held my peace' is an English idiom for staying quiet, and it turns the Hebrew Hiphil, 'I made myself still', into a figure of speech. The Hebrew is an act of will, with an effort in it that the idiom smooths over. 'My sorrow was stirred' is also gentle: ne'kar is the verb of muddying and disturbing (Metzudat Zion cites Gen 34:30, 'you have troubled me'), and the pain is churned up like sediment, not merely felt.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil of chashah: 'I made myself quiet', 'I kept still'. The causative form shows the silence as something the speaker does to himself. English 'held my peace' makes it an idiom.
'Away from good': he withholds even good speech, so that nothing bad can slip out with it. Radak also offers a second reading, that he has no good left to speak of.
Niphal of 'akhar, 'to trouble, stir up, foul'. The picture is of water or soil churned up. Metzudat Zion links it to 'you have troubled me' (Gen 34:30).

verses.translation_literal: Hot [became] my heart within me; in my sighing a fire burns; I spoke with my tongue:
verses.translation_dramatic: But the heat rose inside me. My heart burned in my chest, and the more I muttered to myself the fiercer the fire grew, until at last my tongue broke loose, and I spoke.
verses.directors_commentary: The muzzle fails, and the failure is physical. The heart is not the seat of emotion alone but of thought and will; it 'became hot' (cham) within the speaker's inner organs (qerev). The pivot is hagig, which the KJV renders 'musing'. It is a low murmuring, a half-voiced sound of the kind we make under our breath, and Metzudat David reads it as the breath leaving the mouth, burning hot like fire. 'Musing' is too calm, 'sighing' or 'murmuring' is closer. The fire is the pain of verse 3 still stirring, now ignited by his own held-in words. Then comes the sentence the whole psalm turns on, 'I spoke with my tongue', in which the sinful tongue of verse 2 is named again, bilshoni, as if to show the vow broken in the same breath. Radak and Ibn Ezra note that the phrase repeats the idea 'I spoke'. The KJV 'then spake I' adds a 'then' that Hebrew does not need; the Hebrew simply sets the verb after the fire. Deliver it as a gasp, after a long pause.

philological_notes.note: A low murmur or sigh, related to hagah 'to murmur, meditate'. 'Musing' (KJV) makes it quiet thinking; here it is half-spoken sound. Metzudat Zion links it to hegyon, 'speech, utterance'.
'I spoke with my tongue': the redundancy is deliberate (Ibn Ezra, Radak). It echoes the vow 'from sinning with my tongue' in verse 2.

verses.translation_literal: Make me know, YHWH, my end, and the measure of my days, what it [is]; let me know how fleeting I [am].
verses.translation_dramatic: LORD, let me know my end. Tell me the measure of my days, how much is left of them, so that I may learn how short-lived, how fleeting, I am.
verses.directors_commentary: What bursts out is not a curse, nor the complaint the wicked were waiting for. It is a request for arithmetic. 'My end' (qitzi) is the limit of the lifespan, and 'the measure' (middat) is something measured with a rod or cord. Radak's reading is the key to the speaker's mood: if the span is long he will endure until healed; if short, let him die quickly, for he cannot bear this pain with nothing beyond it. The KJV 'that I may know' makes the second clause a purpose; the Hebrew has the plain cohortative 'let me know', and also takes a different word for 'frail': chadel. It is a rare adjective from the verb meaning 'to cease', so literally 'how ceasing am I', or 'how transient'. Radak and Metzudat Zion connect it to the 'inhabitants of chaled' (Isa 38:11), the transient world. The KJV 'frail' is acceptable, though it drifts toward weakness of body; the Hebrew speaks of duration. Tone: low, not defiant; a man tired of shouting.

philological_notes.note: An adjective from 'to cease': 'ceasing, transient, lacking'. Metzudat Zion and Ibn Ezra link it to cheled 'world, lifespan' by reversal of letters (compare Isa 38:11); Meiri also derives it from 'inhabitants of chaled'. 'Frail' (KJV) shifts the sense toward weakness.
'The measure of my days': a length measured out. It sets up the handbreadth image of the next verse.

verses.translation_literal: Behold, handbreadths you have made my days, and my lifespan [is] like nothing before you. Surely all vanity [is] every person set up. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look: you have made my days a handful of fingers' widths, and all my years are nothing at all before you. Every living man, standing upright, is only breath. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: The answer arrives as an image, and it is a measurement. A tefach is a handbreadth, the width of four fingers, about 8 to 10 centimeters, the smallest standard length of the biblical system, which is the point. The KJV 'as an handbreadth' is singular and sets it as a comparison; the Hebrew is plural and there is no 'as': 'you have made my days handbreadths'. Rashi: days are measured, like something measured in spans. 'My lifespan' (cheldi) is the same word-family as chadel in verse 5, so the question is answered in its own word. 'Before you' means 'in your sight'. Then the key word of the psalm, hevel: the KJV 'vanity' is a church word. Literally it is breath, a puff of steam, the vapor of a breath on a cold morning. 'Every man at his best state' (KJV) is a famous overreach: nitsav means simply 'set up, standing', so 'every man standing', in the strongest pose, is still just a breath. Selah is a pause marker of uncertain meaning; here it falls after the statement, so leave the silence.

philological_notes.note: Plural of tefach, a handbreadth (four fingers, the smallest unit of length). Used of measurement (Rashi, Metzudat David: 'measured as something measured by a handbreadth').
Literally breath, vapor; figuratively what is insubstantial and quickly gone. The same word is Qohelet's refrain; Radak reads 'all hevel' as 'hevel of hevels' (Eccl 1:2). Also the name Abel.
'Set up, standing'. The KJV 'at his best state' interprets the posture as strength; Ibn Ezra reads it as fixed and never changing.

verses.translation_literal: Surely in a shadow-image a person goes about; surely [for] vanity they are in turmoil; he heaps up and does not know who [will be] gathering them.
verses.translation_dramatic: We walk through life as shadows, as outlines of ourselves, and for what? For breath. We scurry and roar and pile up our stores, and never know whose hands will gather them in.
verses.directors_commentary: Three images in one breath. First, tselem: 'image', 'shadow', or 'outline'. The KJV 'vain shew' (a vain show) takes the sense of a mere appearance, which is a defensible reading, and the speaker's point is that the person is a projection with nothing solid behind it. Rashi, Radak and Meiri take it as 'darkness' (compare tsalmavet), walking blind to the day of death; Ibn Ezra, as a changing form, like a river whose reflection stays while the water goes. Second, the verb yehemayun is a word for roaring and crowds, the noise of a city, and Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read it as the clamour of acquiring wealth: the KJV 'disquieted' is correct but pale. Third, the picture of the farmer or the merchant who heaps (yitsbor) grain or silver and does not know 'who will gather them', as the harvest is gathered into the house (Rashi, Metzudat Zion). In an agrarian economy that stings, because land and stores stay in the family; he does not even know whose family. The KJV adds 'riches', which the Hebrew leaves out.

philological_notes.note: 'In an image/shadow'. Disputed: 'darkness' (Rashi, Radak, Meiri), a changing form (Ibn Ezra), 'image of God' (Targum). KJV 'a vain shew' takes it as an unreal appearance.
'They roar, they are in uproar': the noise of a crowd. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion connect it to hamon in the sense of amassing wealth.

verses.translation_literal: And now, what have I waited for, Lord? My hope, to you it [is].
verses.translation_dramatic: And now? What is left for me to wait for, Lord? Nothing in the world I have looked at. My hope, all of it, is turned toward you.
verses.directors_commentary:
The Psalm turns on this verse. After 'every man is a breath' and the heaped-up wealth that someone else will gather, the speaker asks what is left to wait for, and answers with one word order: 'to you it is'. The pronoun hi', 'it', is a small hinge: my hope, that thing, belongs to you. The line is spoken quietly, after the long bitterness of vv. 5-7, not shouted as a victory.

The KJV ('what wait I for? my hope is in thee') is faithful in sense but archaic in word order. It also softens the double vocabulary: two different words for waiting and hope, qiviti and tochalti, both from the vocabulary of stretching toward something, as of a rope pulled taut. Radak reads the line as a patient's turning from physicians to God: his only hope is in the Lord, not in healers. Rashi takes it as a request: from my sins, rescue me, which leads straight into v. 9.

philological_notes.note: A rare noun for 'hope, expectation', found in Proverbs, Lamentations and Job. It belongs to the same family as the verb yachal, 'to wait', and Metzudat Zion glosses it simply as 'my hope'. Beside qiviti, 'I waited', it makes hope heard twice in one line.
Piel perfect of qavah, 'to wait for, hope', a verb whose root image is a stretched cord. Here it asks 'what is there for me to hope in?', and the next clause answers.

verses.translation_literal: From all my transgressions deliver me; [the] reproach of [the] fool do not make me.
verses.translation_dramatic: Rescue me from every one of my wrongs. And do not make me the laughingstock of a fool.
verses.directors_commentary: Now the speaker admits his case: 'transgressions' (pesha'im) are not accidents but acts of rebellion, the strongest of the Hebrew words for wrongdoing; the KJV 'transgressions' is exact. Ibn Ezra and Radak read them as the cause of the illness. In the second line, the fool is a nabal, not a stupid man but a morally bankrupt one, as in the story of Nabal in 1 Samuel 25, whose name is his character. 'The reproach of the fool' means the mockery a nabal can heap on the sufferer, and it connects back to verse 2: the 'wicked before me' is the very person whose jeers he feared (Radak). To the ancient ear, disease was proof of guilt, so the sick man's real horror is that those who watch him will say, 'See what he deserved.' KJV 'make me not the reproach' is faithful but the word order, 'reproach of the fool', is kept in Hebrew for emphasis.

philological_notes.note: A fool in the moral and religious sense, not merely stupid (compare Ps 14:1, and Nabal in 1 Sam 25). KJV 'foolish' is a little mild.
Transgressions, rebellions: the strongest of the Hebrew words for sin. Ibn Ezra and Radak say they are the cause of the illness.

verses.translation_literal: I have been struck dumb; I will not open my mouth, for you [are the one who] has done [it].
verses.translation_dramatic: I have gone mute. I will not open my mouth. You did this.
verses.directors_commentary: The silence of verse 3 returns, but it has changed its meaning: there it was fear of the onlooker, here it is submission before God. The same verb, ne'elamti, opens both verses, and the repetition ties the psalm together. The final clause, ki attah asita, is only three words in Hebrew: 'for you, you have done'. The KJV 'because thou didst it' has the right sense but loses the blunt force of the pronoun 'you' placed first. What did God do? The Hebrew does not say 'it': that object is supplied by every English version and by the commentators, who differ on it. Radak and Metzudat David: the illness and punishment, and a righteous judge does no wrong; Malbim: the speaker's own making, ('you made me'). The silence is neither peace nor triumph. It is a mouth shut by a hand he cannot argue with. Say it almost without voice.

philological_notes.note: 'For you have done [it]'. The object is not stated. Radak: the suffering comes from God, not people, so there is no one to cry out against; Malbim: 'you made me'.

verses.translation_literal: Remove from upon me your plague; from the contending of your hand I have come to an end.
verses.translation_dramatic: Take your plague off me. Under the blows of your hand, I am finished.
verses.directors_commentary: The silence breaks once more, this time as a plea to the one he refuses to accuse. 'Your plague' (nig'ekha) is the word for a blow or a mark of disease, the same word used of the 'plague' of leprosy in Leviticus 13; the KJV 'stroke' is softer. 'The hostility of your hand' is the hard phrase: tigrat is attested only here, and the sense 'contending, quarrel, attack' comes from the root meaning to provoke battle (Rashi, from 2 Chr 25:19; Deut 2:5, quoted by Radak and Metzudat Zion). The KJV 'the blow of thine hand' makes it a single strike; the Hebrew sees a hand that is fighting him. Ibn Ezra and Rashi's quoted authority take it as 'fear' from the root gur. 'I have come to an end' (chaliti) is a verb of finishing, used for a consumed supply; KJV 'consumed' is good. 'Hand' is God's agency: a sick man in the ancient world experienced illness as being struck. Deliver the last words as breath running out.

philological_notes.note: A blow or a visible mark of disease; the same word is the biblical 'plague' of skin disease (Lev 13). Radak: the suffix can denote the one who suffers the plague, not only the sender.
Found only here. Derived from the verb 'to contend, provoke' (Rashi, Radak, Metzudat Zion) or from 'to fear' (Ibn Ezra); the first reading gives 'the contending of your hand'.

verses.translation_literal: With rebukes for iniquity you have disciplined a person, and you have melted away, like the moth, his desired thing. Surely vanity [is] every person. Selah.
verses.translation_dramatic: With rebukes you correct a man for his guilt, and what he most prized you eat away, as a moth eats cloth. Every one of us is only breath. Selah.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm now states its theology, and the speaker steps back from himself to speak of 'a person' (ish). 'Rebukes' (tochachot) and 'disciplined' (yissarta) are the vocabulary of a parent teaching a child, and the Hebrew verb is the same one for a father's correction in Proverbs; Rashi connects the rebukes to the curses of Leviticus 26 and Deuteronomy 28. The second line is the image everyone remembers: God melts away 'his desired thing' (chamudo) as a moth does. The KJV 'beauty' is a guess; chamudo is whatever a man craves, his health, his body, his wealth (Rashi: his flesh; Metzudat David: his riches), and the ancients feared moths because they destroyed cloth, the stored wealth of a household, as in Isaiah 50:9. The verb temes means to dissolve or make melt, hence to cause to waste away. The final line repeats verse 6 almost word for word, 'surely vanity every person', a refrain that closes the argument on the same note and with another Selah; the KJV 'surely every man is vanity' loses the repeated 'akh' that opens the verse both times. Let the second Selah hang longer than the first.

philological_notes.note: 'His desired thing': what a person craves. Read as his body (Rashi, Ibn Ezra), his flesh (Radak) or his wealth (Metzudat David). KJV 'beauty' chooses one.
'Like the moth', the clothes moth whose larvae eat cloth. Metzudat Zion: the worm that consumes a garment.
Rebukes, reproofs; Metzudat Zion links it to the sufferings of Job 33:19 ('and he is chastened with pain').

verses.translation_literal: Hear my prayer, YHWH, and to my cry for help give ear; to my tear do not be silent. For a ger I [am] with you, a toshav, like all my fathers.
verses.translation_dramatic: Hear my prayer, O LORD. Listen to my cry. Do not be deaf and quiet before my tears; I have been silent long enough, and now it is You who must not be. For I am a guest in Your land, a stranger who has been let in to stay, as every one of my fathers was.
verses.directors_commentary:
The silence the speaker kept in vv. 3 and 10 is answered here with a plea that God not keep silence: 'do not be silent' uses the root charash, the opposite of the speaker's own restraint. Three pleas climb in intensity: prayer, cry for help, tear. The last is the strongest because a tear needs no words. Ibn Ezra calls prayer and tear together like a physician's medicine.

The KJV has 'hold not thy peace at my tears', which is fair, though 'hold not thy peace' recalls its own 'held my peace' in v. 3 and so hides that the Hebrew uses a different root here. The closing 'stranger ... sojourner' is also the right pair of words, but modern readers hear 'stranger' as just 'unfamiliar person'. A ger is a resident outsider who owns no land of his own and lives under a host's protection. A toshav is a settled alien, someone who has put down a dwelling (Metzudat Zion calls it the 'reverse' of ger, Radak says it is called 'toshav' because he settles in for what seems a long stay). The pair says: I have no ground here, and what I do have, I have by Your hospitality. The word 'with you' ('immakh) completes the picture: the host is God.

The line reaches back to Lev 25:23, where God says the land is His and Israel are 'gerim and toshavim with Me', a link Ibn Ezra supports with 'as written in the Torah'. Radak adds 1 Chr 29:15, 'we are strangers before you and sojourners, as all our fathers were', and reads it as the human condition in this world: a brief stay under God's roof, the same for every generation.

philological_notes.note: A resident outsider without land of his own, who lives under the protection of a host. Here the host is God. The link to Lev 25:23, where Israel are called gerim and toshavim 'with Me', is attested by Ibn Ezra's remark that this is as it is written in the Torah.
A settled alien, someone who lives in a place without belonging to it. Metzudat Zion calls it the reverse of ger; Radak explains the name as 'one who settles', as if for a long stay in this world.
'Do not be silent', the opposite of the speaker's vows of silence in vv. 3 and 10. The speaker has been quiet; now he asks that God not be.

verses.translation_literal: Look away from me, so that I may brighten, before I go, and I am not.
verses.translation_dramatic: Look away from me. Only for a little while; lift your hand and let me breathe. Let the colour come back into my face and let me smile once more, before I go, before I am gone, and nothing of me is left anywhere.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm ends not with trust but with a request to be left alone. 'Look away' is a daring thing to say to God: in the rest of the Bible God's look is a blessing, and here the speaker begs him to turn his gaze aside, because that gaze is what is crushing him (see v. 11–12, 'the blow of your hand', 'rebukes', the moth). KJV's 'O spare me' turns an image into a formula, and the verb underneath, הָשַׁע, is not 'spare' at all. Rashi, Ibn Ezra and Metzudat Zion read it as 'turn away, stay your hand from striking me'. The Hebrew is blunt, almost rude, and a good actor should play it that way, with exhaustion rather than politeness.

The second verb, אַבְלִיגָה, is rarer and gentler. KJV says 'recover strength', which follows Rashi and Ibn Ezra, who take it as 'grow strong again'. But the root בלג is about a face lighting up, as in Job 9:27, 'I will brighten'. The man is not asking to run again but to be cheerful for a moment. The ending is also stark: וְאֵינֶנִּי, 'and I am not'. KJV's 'and be no more' is fair, but the Hebrew is more abrupt, just 'there is not-me'. In Israel's thinking, the dead go down to Sheol and no longer take part in the life God can see; Radak and Meiri cite Ecclesiastes 9:10, 'there is no work or knowledge in Sheol', and read the plea as a wish to do God's will while there is still time. The audience should hear both the dread and the strangely small hope in the line.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil imperative of שָׁעָה 'to gaze': 'make your gaze turn aside'. Rashi says 'stay your hand from striking me', Ibn Ezra compares Isaiah 22:4 שְׁעוּ מִנִּי and Metzudat Zion explains 'turn away'. STEPBible's 'smear' is a different root and does not fit.
Cohortative of בָּלַג: 'let me brighten, let me show cheer'. Rashi and Ibn Ezra take it as 'grow strong'; Radak as recovering from illness so as to do God's will again.
'And I am not': the particle אֵין 'there is not' with a first-person suffix. It states non-existence, not just death, and Radak links it to Ecclesiastes 9:10.
